## 1. Research objective
- [A] To systematically evaluate how well pre-trained LLMs detect known security vulnerabilities across more datasets, languages, models, prompts and vulnerability classes than prior work, and to compare them with a static analyser (CodeQL) and deep-learning detectors (DeepDFA, LineVul) (p. 1–3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: LLM performance across languages and datasets; RQ2: effect of prompting strategies; RQ3: variation across vulnerability classes (CWEs); RQ4: LLMs vs state-of-the-art static analysis; RQ5: LLMs vs state-of-the-art DL tools (Table I, p. 2). No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Function/snippet-level binary classification benchmark on balanced samples, plus manual qualitative inspection of 20-sample subsets (p. 3–6).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 16 pre-trained LLMs, "Instruct" variants where available: Qwen-2.5-Coder 1.5B/7B, CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, DeepSeekCoder 7B/15B(v2)/33B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B, Qwen-2.5 14B/32B, Codestral-22B, Gemini-1.5-Flash, GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) (Table V, p. 4). [V] Three prompts with a "security researcher" persona: Basic (any vulnerability), CWE-specific (target CWE named), CWE-DF (simulate source–sink–sanitizer dataflow analysis before the verdict) (p. 4, p. 14). [V] Few-shot and chain-of-thought were tried with GPT-4 on 100 samples and dropped as not better than CWE-DF (p. 4, p. 14–15). No fine-tuning of LLMs.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] CodeQL with official queries for the Top-25 CWEs, on synthetic datasets only (OWASP, Juliet Java, Juliet C/C++) because real-world projects need building (p. 7–8). [V] DeepDFA (GNN over CFG + dataflow facts) and LineVul (transformer) from DeepDFA's artifact, trained on Juliet C/C++, CVEFixes C/C++ (test samples excluded) or BigVul, 80/20 train/validation, tested on the 1,000 CVEFixes C/C++ samples, averaged over three runs (p. 9). CodeQL version: not reported.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] OWASP Benchmark (Java, synthetic), SARD Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ (synthetic), CVEFixes Java and C/C++ (real-world, method-level from NVD fix commits) (Table III, p. 3). [V] CVEFixes chosen because it has CVE/CWE metadata, is two-sided and multi-language (p. 3).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 5,000 code snippets: 1,000 per dataset, 500 vulnerable + 500 non-vulnerable; 25 CWEs (p. 1, p. 5; Table VI, p. 4). Unit = single method/snippet.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Filtering: Top-25 CWE only, snippets ≤2,048 tokens, multi-file Juliet cases skipped, then random sampling (Table VI, p. 4; p. 5; p. 14). [V] Hints removed: comments stripped, identifying names (e.g., "CWE80_XSS…", "owasp") anonymised (p. 5, p. 14). [V] CVEFixes labels: pre-fix vs post-fix versions of methods changed in fix commits (p. 14).
- Data availability (public? link?): source datasets public (p. 3); the authors' sampled subsets and evaluation code: not reported (no link in this version).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] OpenAI ChatCompletions API (GPT-3.5/4), Gemini API, Hugging Face for open models on a cluster with A100, A6000 and RTX 2080 GPUs; temperature 0, max 1,024 output tokens, top-1 prediction, default other parameters (p. 5). [V] Single run per benchmark (p. 10). [A] CWE-DF "is costlier since it generates more tokens" (p. 4). Token counts, monetary cost, runtime: not reported.
- Code availability: not reported in this version.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 as standard classification metrics (p. 3–4). [V] Balanced accuracy per CWE for RQ3/RQ4, only CWEs with ≥10 samples, best prompt per model and dataset (p. 6–7). [V] RQ1 reports the best accuracy/F1 per model per dataset across prompts (p. 5).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported; [A] "significantly" is used descriptively (p. 1); standard-deviation bars across models in Fig. 2 (p. 5).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Best model+prompt per dataset averages 62.8% accuracy; bests are Llama-3.1-70B (CWE) 76% on Juliet Java, Qwen-2.5-14B 65% on Juliet C/C++, CodeLlama-13B 60% on OWASP, Gemini-1.5-Flash 57% on CVEFixes Java, Qwen-2.5-32B 56% on CVEFixes C/C++ (p. 5). [A] Mean F1 0.71 (p. 1–2).
2. [V] Best accuracies on synthetic datasets are 10.5% higher on average than on real-world datasets (p. 5).
3. [A] Performance does not improve with scale: Qwen-2.5-14B/32B beat GPT-x on real-world data; only GPT-x and Llama-3.1-x improve with size on ≥3 datasets (p. 5).
4. [V] CWE-DF raises average F1 over CWE and Basic prompts on real-world datasets by up to 0.18 (CVEFixes C/C++) and 0.14 (CVEFixes Java), with lowest variance across models (p. 5). [V] Basic prompt names an incorrect CWE in >60% (Java) and >53% (C/C++) of samples (p. 6; Table VII).
5. [V] Manual inspection (20-sample subsets): CWE-DF identifies correct sources/sinks in 18/20 and sanitizers in 16/20 real-world Java samples; on wrongly predicted Juliet C/C++ samples, sources/sinks/sanitizers are correct in 17/20 but unsanitized flows wrong in 12/20 (p. 6).
6. [V] CWE-wise: best on self-contained vulnerabilities — CWE-78 (Llama-3.1-70B 64% CVEFixes Java, 78% CVEFixes C/C++), CWE-787/125 in Java (Llama-3.1-8B/GPT-4 up to 89%/84%), CWE-476 (DSCoder-7B 63–88%), CWE-89 (GPT-3.5 70% on CVEFixes Java), CWE-79 (Qwen-2.5-32B 66–67%); poor on CWE-862 and on C/C++ out-of-bounds (<53% for GPT-4/Llama-3.1-8B; no LLM >60%) (p. 7).
7. [V] CodeQL vs best LLM per synthetic dataset (A/P/R/F1): OWASP 0.63/0.58/0.96/0.72 vs CodeLlama-13B 0.60/0.58/0.74/0.65; Juliet Java 0.94/0.92/0.95/0.94 vs Llama-3.1-70B 0.76/0.71/0.89/0.79; Juliet C/C++ 0.72/0.99/0.44/0.61 vs Qwen-2.5-14B 0.65/0.60/0.89/0.72 (Table VIII, p. 9). CodeQL has higher accuracy on all three; the LLM has higher F1 only on Juliet C/C++ (p. 8).
8. [V] LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-22, CWE-78, CWE-476, CWE-416 on ≥2 of 3 datasets (e.g., DSCoder-7B +24% on CWE-416 Juliet C/C++; +12% on CWE-476 Juliet Java); CodeQL beats LLMs on CWE-190 by 11% (Juliet Java) and 21% (Juliet C/C++) (p. 8). [A] CodeQL misses some cases because its queries are narrow (e.g., CWE-78 query handles execl but not _execvp) (p. 8).
9. [V] DL tools on CVEFixes C/C++ (A/P/R/F1): DeepDFA trained in-distribution 0.51/0.55/0.17/0.23; LineVul in-distribution 0.59/0.58/0.65/0.61; Qwen-2.5-32B (CWE-DF, no training) 0.56/0.54/0.81/0.65. Trained on BigVul, both reach ≥0.98 accuracy on BigVul but LineVul drops to 0.50/0.63/0.01/0.02 on CVEFixes (Table IX, p. 10). [A] DL tools do not generalise across datasets; LLMs preferable for low inference overhead and explanations (p. 9–10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Choice of LLMs and datasets may bias results; may not generalise to other languages or datasets (p. 10).
- [A] Single runs; GPT-3.5/GPT-4 may be non-deterministic even at temperature 0 (p. 10).
- [A] Possible bugs in evaluation code and errors in manual analysis, mitigated by multiple co-authors' review (p. 10).
- [A] Multi-file samples and snippets >2,048 tokens excluded due to prompt size (p. 5, p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Headline F1 is close to a trivial baseline: on 50/50 balanced data, always answering "vulnerable" gives P = 0.50, R = 1.00, F1 = 0.67, and many configurations show exactly this pattern (e.g., CodeLlama-7B, CodeLlama-13B, CodeLlama-34B and DSCoder-15B with CWE-DF: A 0.50 / P 0.50 / R 1.00 / F1 0.67 on most datasets, Table XII, p. 16). The mean F1 of 0.71 therefore says little; accuracy (~50–60%) is the more honest signal.
- [I] Best-of-48 selection: RQ1 and RQ4 report the best model+prompt per dataset chosen after seeing test results (p. 5, p. 8), which favours LLMs against a single CodeQL configuration.
- [I] CodeQL is compared only on synthetic Juliet/OWASP data, where CodeQL queries are well-tuned, and LLM–CodeQL comparison on real-world code is absent (p. 7–8). This limits RQ1/RQ4 conclusions for real code.
- [I] Balanced 50/50 evaluation does not reflect real-world prevalence of vulnerable code; precision would drop sharply at realistic ratios.
- [I] Data contamination: Juliet, OWASP and CVEFixes are public and predate the LLMs' training cut-offs; not discussed beyond identifier anonymisation (p. 5, p. 14).
- [I] CVEFixes method-level labels are known to be noisy (fix-commit heuristic); label quality is not assessed. The appendix sentence labelling methods "in the fix commit and the parent commit … as vulnerable and non-vulnerable, respectively" (p. 14) reads reversed relative to the usual convention; likely a wording error.
- [I] Table V lists "DSCoder-15B" as deepseekcoder-v2-15b with size "33B" (p. 4), an internal inconsistency.
- [I] The abstract's statement that LLMs report higher accuracies than CodeQL refers to specific CWEs only; overall CodeQL wins on accuracy on all three synthetic datasets (p. 1 vs p. 8).
- [I] No cost or runtime data, so trade-offs for RQ3 cannot be assessed.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Post-hoc best-configuration selection; possible pre-training contamination; DL tools trained with 80/20 split but tested on the same 1,000-sample set as LLMs (CVEFixes test samples excluded from training, p. 9).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Function-level snippets only, no inter-procedural/multi-file context; two languages; Top-25 CWEs; balanced sampling.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Binary verdict ignores whether the predicted CWE or location is right (Basic prompt names wrong CWE >53–60% of the time, p. 6); F1 on balanced data inflated by "always yes" behaviour.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] 1,000 samples per dataset is reasonable, but per-CWE analysis uses as few as 10 samples (p. 7); no significance tests or CIs; single runs.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Prompts fully given (p. 14–15) and model versions listed (p. 4); sampled subsets and code not linked in this arXiv version.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: neuro-symbolic techniques combining LLM reasoning with logical reasoning engines and static analyzers (p. 11); use LLMs to infer specifications (sources, sinks, sanitizers) that static analysis then reasons over (p. 6, p. 8–10).
- Suggested by us [I]: evaluate CodeQL and LLMs together on real-world code at realistic prevalence; report trivial baselines; test the proposed LLM-specification + static-analysis hybrid directly.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: Peer-reviewed (ICST 2025), multi-dataset study that covers all three families (LLM, SAST via CodeQL, DL via DeepDFA/LineVul). It shows CodeQL still wins overall on synthetic suites while LLMs win particular CWEs, and that LLM F1 on balanced data can be near-trivial. It is a key source for RQ4 (CWE-specific strengths) and for the "LLM finds specs, static analysis reasons" hybrid idea in RQ3/RQ5.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Best LLM+prompt per dataset averages 62.8% accuracy on balanced function-level data; real-world accuracy 10.5% lower than synthetic | 5 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | CodeQL beats the best LLM in accuracy on OWASP (0.63 vs 0.60), Juliet Java (0.94 vs 0.76) and Juliet C/C++ (0.72 vs 0.65); F1: CodeQL 0.72/0.94/0.61 vs LLM 0.65/0.79/0.72 | 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | On CVEFixes C/C++, Qwen-2.5-32B (prompted) F1 0.65 vs in-distribution-trained DeepDFA 0.23 and LineVul 0.61; LineVul trained on BigVul collapses to F1 0.02 on CVEFixes | 10 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Model scale does not reliably improve detection; Qwen-2.5-14B/32B beat GPT-4 on real-world data | 5 | A | moderate |
| RQ2 | Many LLM configurations behave as "always vulnerable" (P 0.50, R 1.00, F1 0.67) on 50/50 data, so F1 ≈ trivial baseline | 16 | I | moderate |
| RQ2 | CodeQL evaluated only on synthetic datasets; best LLM configuration chosen post hoc from 16 models × 3 prompts | 5, 7–8 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | CWE-DF (dataflow-style) prompt raises real-world F1 by up to 0.18; LLMs correctly identify sources/sinks/sanitizers in 16–18 of 20 inspected samples even when the verdict is wrong | 5–6 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Authors propose neuro-symbolic hybrids: LLMs infer specifications, static analysers reason over them | 8–11 | A | weak |
| RQ4 | LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-22, CWE-78, CWE-476, CWE-416 (e.g., +24% on CWE-416); CodeQL better on CWE-190 (+11–21%) | 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | LLMs do well on self-contained CWEs (78, 476, 89, 79, Java 125/787) and poorly on context-dependent ones (CWE-862, C/C++ out-of-bounds with structs/pointers) | 7 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Missing global/inter-procedural context is the main failure cause on real-world C/C++; multi-file samples excluded | 5, 7 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "LLMs report lower overall accuracies than CodeQL on all synthetic datasets." (p. 2)

> "the best accuracies on synthetic datasets are 10.5% higher on average than those on the real-world datasets" (p. 5)

> "Finding 3.2: Poor performance on real-world C/C++ is due to missing global context." (p. 7)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read including appendix (pp. 1–18) and the full metrics table (Table XII, p. 16). Figures 1–4 are images; their numbers were taken from the text, not read off the plots.
- Source version: arXiv v3 (2311.16169, 23 Oct 2024). Published version: ICST 2025 (DOI 10.1109/icst62969.2025.10988968, from metadata). Numbers may differ slightly from the camera-ready; recheck if the published PDF becomes available.
- Uncertainties: the abstract's mean F1 0.71 is not directly traceable to a single table cell (likely the mean of best-per-model F1s in Fig. 1). Whether code/data were released is not stated in this version.

[V] Three prompts with a "security researcher" persona: Basic (any vulnerability), CWE-specific (target CWE named), CWE-DF (simulate source–sink–sanitizer dataflow analysis before the verdict) (p. 4, p. 14). [V] Few-shot and chain-of-thought were tried with GPT-4 on 100 samples and dropped as not better than CWE-DF (p. 4, p. 14–15). No fine-tuning of LLMs.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] CodeQL with official queries for the Top-25 CWEs, on synthetic datasets only (OWASP, Juliet Java, Juliet C/C++) because real-world projects need building (p. 7–8). [V] DeepDFA (GNN over CFG + dataflow facts) and LineVul (transformer) from DeepDFA's artifact, trained on Juliet C/C++, CVEFixes C/C++ (test samples excluded) or BigVul, 80/20 train/validation, tested on the 1,000 CVEFixes C/C++ samples, averaged over three runs (p. 9). CodeQL version: not reported.

33	                                               Abstract. Identifying vulnerabilities in source code is crucial, especially
34	                                               in critical software components. Existing methods such as static analy-
35	                                               sis, dynamic analysis, formal verification, and recently Large Language
36	                                               Models are widely used to detect security flaws. This paper introduces
37	                                               CASTLE (CWE Automated Security Testing and Low-Level Evalua-
38	                                               tion), a benchmarking framework for evaluating the vulnerability detec-
39	                                               tion capabilities of different methods. We assess 13 static analysis tools,
40	                                               10 LLMs, and 2 formal verification tools using a hand-crafted dataset of
41	                                               250 micro-benchmark programs covering 25 common CWEs. We propose
42	                                               the CASTLE Score, a novel evaluation metric for fair comparison. Our
43	                                               results reveal key differences: ESBMC (a formal verification tool) min-
44	                                               imizes false positives but struggles with vulnerabilities beyond model
45	                                               checking, such as weak cryptography or SQL injection. Static analyz-
46	                                               ers suffer from high false positives, increasing manual validation efforts
47	                                               for developers. LLMs perform exceptionally well in the CASTLE dataset
48	                                               when identifying vulnerabilities in small code snippets. However, their ac-
49	                                               curacy declines, and hallucinations increase as the code size grows. These
50	                                               results suggest that LLMs could play a pivotal role in future security so-
51	                                               lutions, particularly within code completion frameworks, where they can
52	                                               provide real-time guidance to prevent vulnerabilities. The dataset is ac-
53	                                               cessible at https://github.com/CASTLE-Benchmark .

59	                                         1    Introduction
60	                                         Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have sparked both excitement
61	                                         and concern about the future of traditional software engineering. For instance,
62	                                         Meta’s recent announcement that AI could soon replace many software engi-
63	                                         neering roles highlights a shifting landscape in code development [1]. While AI-
64	                                         driven code generation offers remarkable efficiency, a study by Tihanyi et al.
65

69	
70	found that all examined large language models (LLMs) produced vulnerable C
71	code [2]. Similar conclusions have been reached in studies examining other pro-
72	gramming languages, such as PHP and Python [3,4]. These large-scale studies
73	consistently indicate that such vulnerabilities arise partly because LLMs lack
74	contextual understanding during the generation process. Several studies high-
75	light that once the code is generated, and a vulnerability is identified, LLMs
76	excel in fixing these [5,6]. The question is, how do we find the vulnerabilities?
77	Despite the growing importance of automated software verification, developers
78	and security practitioners lack clear guidance on which tools are most reliable
79	for detecting vulnerabilities in C code. Several interrelated issues contribute to
80	this uncertainty:
81	    1. Diverse vulnerability types. Security flaws in C code range from classic memory
82	       management issues (e.g., buffer overflows) to subtler logical errors. We need to
83	       understand which detection methods can reliably detect different categories.
84	    2. Emergence of LLMs. While LLMs exhibit promise in automated code genera-
85	       tion, bug fixing, and vulnerability detection, their reliability in different vulnera-
86	       bilities and coding scenarios is unclear.
87	    3. Lack of standardized benchmarks. Existing datasets often contain too many
88	       samples with imbalanced CWE representations, and fail to represent the breadth
89	       of CWE vulnerabilities. Tools that rely on compilable code—particularly FV meth-
90	       ods—are especially disadvantaged without realistic, fully functional programs. To
91	       gauge each tool’s performance accurately, a benchmark must be rigorously vali-
92	       dated, contain clearly labeled vulnerabilities, and support line-level detection gran-
93	       ularity.
94	   Given these challenges, a robust and compilable benchmark dataset that
95	accurately captures major CWE vulnerabilities is paramount to answer the fol-
96	lowing research questions:
97	
98	        – RQ1: How do state-of-the-art static analysis tools, formal verification
99	          methods, and LLM-based approaches compare to effectively detecting
100	          C code vulnerabilities?
101	        – RQ2: Are combinations of tools more effective than using a single
102	          tool?
103	        – RQ3: What metrics can reliably demonstrate these differences among
104	          various tools?
105	
106	      Our study holds the following contributions:
107	    – We introduce CASTLE (CWE Automated Security Testing and Low-
108	      Level Evaluation), a curated collection of 250 compilable, compact C programs,
109	      each containing a single CWE. This benchmark is aimed at enabling direct compar-
110	      isons among current and future vulnerability scanning tools, including traditional
111	      static analyzers, FV techniques, and LLM-based approaches.
112	    – We conduct a broad comparison of the most widely used static code analyzers and
113	      popular LLMs to assess their effectiveness in detecting important vulnerabilities
114	      in the C language, using a new metric called CASTLE Score, thereby providing
115	      crucial insights into their relative strengths and weaknesses.

131	2     Related work
132	Ensuring software correctness, safety, and security is central to software engineer-
133	ing. Examining related literature on the role of AI in software development, most
134	of the existing work and benchmarking approaches focused on testing LLMs’ ca-
135	pabilities in producing functionally correct code. However, safety and security
136	are just as important.
137	
138	2.1       Datasets and Benchmarks
139	Existing vulnerability datasets are frequently used for fine-tuning machine learn-
140	ing models, yet they exhibit several shortcomings that make them unsuitable for
141	comprehensive benchmarking. First, many datasets offer imbalanced represen-
142	tations of CWE categories, failing to provide adequate test coverage of certain
143	vulnerability types. Second, an extreme or uneven distribution of vulnerable
144	versus non-vulnerable samples either hinders accurate false-positive evaluation
145	(when nearly all samples are vulnerable) or fails to capture diverse false-negative
146	scenarios (when some vulnerability types remain underrepresented).

194	ally, the newly introduced CASTLE score provides a more detailed comparative

197	dataset balances vulnerable and non-vulnerable samples, permitting more robust

200	2.2   Traditional Vulnerability Scanning Overview
201	Traditional approaches have long relied on static analysis methods, such as pat-
202	tern matching, data flow analysis, and taint analysis, as well as dynamic anal-
203	ysis techniques like fuzz testing [16]. Likewise, Formal Verification (FV) meth-
204	ods [17], including Bounded Model Checking (BMC) [18] and theorem proving,
205	are widely employed to detect security flaws such as buffer overflows. The NIST-
206	led Static Analysis Tool Exposition (SATE) [19,20] provided large-scale eval-
207	uations on open-source code, confirming that while these scanners could spot
208	certain weaknesses, no single method excelled across all vulnerability types.
209	    Academic and industrial benchmarks reveal similar shortcomings. Early work
210	by Wilander and Kamkar [21] showed that five tools missed most C function vul-
211	nerabilities and produced many false positives, a trend later echoed by Emanuels-
212	son and Nilsson [22]. Johns and Jodeit [23] demonstrated synthetic benchmarks
213	to distinguish genuine alerts from false alarms, while Bennett [24] reported de-
214	tection rates of 11.2%–26.5% for standard SAST tools, improved to 44.7% by
215	augmenting them with enhanced Semgrep rules.
216	
217	2.3   LLM-Based Vulnerability Detection
218	Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in using Large Language Models
219	(LLMs) for automated vulnerability detection [25,26,27]. Although these models
220

222	
223	                                                      CASTE benchmark           5
224	
225	are often praised for handling diverse code repositories, they primarily rely on
226	pattern-based sequence learning rather than (neuro-)symbolic reasoning. As a
227	result, LLMs can detect certain coding flaws effectively, yet they remain suscep-
228	tible to overlooking complex or context-dependent vulnerabilities.
229	    Recent developments, particularly in decoder-only models such as OpenAI’s
230	ChatGPT and Meta’s Code Llama, highlight a shift in how researchers and
231	practitioners approach vulnerability detection. Their larger context window and
232	on-demand text generation facilitate powerful few-shot or prompt-based strate-
233	gies that, for specific benchmarks, surpass classical fine-tuned detectors. For
234	instance, properly designed chain-of-thought prompts have been reported to in-
235	crease F1 scores on real-world vulnerabilities by providing step-by-step guidance
236	for analyzing the code [4].
237	    Vulnerability detectors typically leverage transformer-based code models trained
238	on massive code corpora spanning multiple languages. These training datasets
239	often contain their share of insecure code, potentially introducing biases or
240	“model collapse” issues [28]. Broadly, transformer models are categorized into
241	three groups [29]:
242	1. Encoder-Only: Used for classification tasks. Early work on vulnerability
243	   detection often fine-tuned these models to label code snippets as “vulnerable”
244	   or “safe.” They generally require full retraining for each new task.
245	2. Encoder–Decoder: Useful for sequence-to-sequence tasks, such as code
246	   summarization or refactoring, but they can also be adapted for classification.
247	3. Decoder-Only: Increasingly favored due to large context windows and flex-
248	   ible in-context learning. These models can be prompted to identify vulner-
249	   abilities (and sometimes even propose potential fixes) without parameter
250	   updates, relying on the knowledge captured during pre-training.
251	    The trend toward decoder-only architectures aligns with industry practices,
252	where state-of-the-art LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) are often served via specialized prompts
253	rather than exhaustive retraining. This approach leverages in-context learning,
254	enabling the model to understand and analyze security issues on demand. Care-
255	fully constructed prompts—such as chain-of-thought instructions—can improve
256	detection accuracy by guiding the model’s attention toward specific code pat-
257	terns or CWE categories [4].
258	    Existing work indicates that LLM-based solutions can outperform traditional
259	static analyzers on well-defined benchmarks [26,27,25]. However, these improve-
260	ments do not translate uniformly across all vulnerability types, and use cases:
261	LLMs often fail at detecting nuanced, multi-function flaws or to interpret exten-
262	sive code segments.

281	3.1   Dataset
282	
283	The CASTLE dataset comprises 250 small programs in C, each crafted man-
284	ually by cybersecurity experts. It encompasses 25 distinct CWEs, with 10 test
285	cases per CWE (6 vulnerable and 4 non-vulnerable). This balanced distribution
286	facilitates focused assessments of each tool’s vulnerability detection capabilities
287	while accurately measuring false positives. In ambiguous cases, experts selected
288	a higher-level CWE category or iteratively refined the test until only the most
289	relevant CWE remained.
290	    Each program was required to compile without errors—although compiler
291	warnings were permitted—as this is a requirement for formal verification tools.
292	All benchmarks were written in C and selected for their capacity to accommodate
293	a wide range of vulnerability types, including intricate memory management
294	issues. Furthermore, each test case was restricted to a single file (with optional
295	external libraries) and designed to contain exactly one or zero vulnerabilities.
296	This structure simplifies the identification of vulnerabilities and helps prevent
297	confusion when validating false positives.
298	    When incorporating the system prompt alongside the source code, the total
299	input tokens across the dataset amount to approximately 115,620 tokens using
300	the cl100k_base encoding scheme. This total reflects the resource considerations
301	required when running evaluations with token-sensitive language models. The
302	dataset was intentionally capped at 250 benchmarks to make thorough manual
303	verification feasible. This rigorous verification process is indispensable for de-
304	tecting false positives and confirming line-level detections. Moreover, this selec-
305	tive approach supports the cost-effective evaluation of computationally intensive
306	tools, including advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-o1, GPT-o3, DeepSeek R1).
307	    The benchmarks exhibit substantial variability in complexity. Code lengths
308	range from 7 to 164 lines, yielding 10, 392 lines (an average of 42 lines). Each
309	includes 1–8 functions (2.2 on average), with cyclomatic complexity values span-
310	ning 1–29 (mean 6.3). Halstead volumes range from approximately 89.9 to over
311	5, 246.7, averaging 1, 104.8.

471	3.3     CASTLE Score
472	In this section, we introduce the CASTLE score, a new metric for evaluating
473	the performance of vulnerability detection tools with the CASTLE-Benchmark.
474	The CASTLE score integrates both true- and false-positive rates, awards bonus
475	points for detecting high-impact vulnerabilities (based on the Top 25 CWEs),
476	and rewards correct identification of non-vulnerable code. By incorporating these
477	factors, the metric better captures a tool’s overall reliability than standard
478	pass/fail evaluations.
479	     Let dn = { d1 , d2 , . . . , dn } denote a dataset of n ∈ N+ micro-benchmark tests.
480	Each test di targets a specific security weakness (e.g., buffer overflow) or contains
481	no vulnerabilities. Let vi denote the correct vulnerability label associated with
482	di . If it does not contain a vulnerability, then vi = ∅ For any given tool t, let
483	t(di ) represent the set of vulnerabilities reported by t when analyzing di .
484	     Bonus Formula: Following the Top 25 CWE list released by MITRE [30],
485	let S : CWE → {1, 2, . . . , 25} ∪ {∞} be a function that returns the rank of a
486	given weakness if it appears in the top 25 list, with S(c) = ∞ assigned to any
487	CWE not in the list. Define bmax = 5 as the maximum bonus for detecting a

527	  However, multiple reported findings (|t(di )| > 1) reduce the score by one for
528	  each, penalizing extraneous detections.
529	– Correct Non-Vulnerability Detection. If the benchmark is non-vulnerable (vi =
530	  ∅) and the tool reports no vulnerabilities, it earns 2 points.
531	– All Other Cases. If the tool misses a vulnerability (failing to report vi ), or
532	  incorrectly flags any vulnerability (including false positives in a non-vulnerable
533	  test), the score is reduced by one for each false-positive finding (−|t(di )|).
534	  Notably, it does not incur additional penalties if the tool reports nothing on
535	  a vulnerable benchmark.
536	
537	3.4   CASTLE Combination Score
538	An additional feature of the CASTLE score is its applicability to tool combina-
539	tions. Specifically, if two or more tools exhibit high overlap in detected CWEs,
540	their combined false positives may outweigh any marginal gain from additional
541	true positives, thus lowering the overall score. Conversely, if tools complement
542	each other’s coverage without substantially increasing false-positive rates, their
543	combination can yield higher net performance.
544	    To compute the CASTLE Combination Score, one considers the union of re-
545	ported vulnerabilities and awards true positives and true negatives once while
546	aggregating penalties for all false positives. This ensures that overlapping detec-
547	tions do not artificially inflate the combined score and that the negative impact
548	of extraneous findings remains cumulative. The combination score can be calcu-
549	lated for an any n number of tool combinations.

772	self-contained C programs. We conjecture that their neural architectures confer

776	detecting common software flaws within compact code segments. However, the
777	next section highlights several limitations and issues for LLMs.

779	
780	5    Limitations
781	
782	Microbenchmark Scope: A fundamental concern with any microbenchmark-based
783	study is its limited scope. Although the CASTLE dataset covers 25 distinct
784	CWEs, each test typically focuses on a single vulnerability in an isolated con-
785	text. Real-world software often exhibits multi-faceted security flaws spanning
786	tens or hundreds of files. Consequently, tools optimized for detecting specific
787	vulnerabilities may perform artificially well on microbenchmarks while missing
788	complex, cross-file weaknesses that only arise in large-scale applications. Regard-
789	less, tools did not perform well on even this small test, indicating that their high
790	false positive rates would be a problem for longer contexts.
791	    Lack of Large Code Samples: Preliminary testing with a synthetic 400+ line
792	C program created by merging multiple non-vulnerable test cases, revealed that
793	LLMs tend to report false positives when dealing with larger codebases. Simi-
794	larly, when one hidden vulnerability was introduced into this combined file, most
795	LLMs failed to detect it reliably, suggesting that these models’ effectiveness may
796	taper off with increasing code length. Formal verification approaches also suffer
797	from scalability issues, such as state explosion, and may require lowered bounds
798	that reduce their thoroughness. By contrast, classical static application security
799	testers (SAST) can handle extensive projects more efficiently, yet their propen-
800	sity for false positives undercuts overall usefulness in large-scale deployments.
801	    Potential Overfitting: Because CASTLE test contents are fixed, tool vendors
802	could theoretically fine-tune their analyzers to excel on known benchmarks, in-
803	flating reported accuracy while not generalizing to unseen software. Although
804	this consideration does not impact the integrity of our current study, it un-
805	derscores the importance of periodically refreshing the dataset or incorporating
806	dynamic test-generation approaches for the future. Furthermore, while repeated
807	evaluations of the same code typically yield consistent results (with observed
808	deviations below 3%), the inherent stochasticity of model-based systems stands
809	in contrast to the deterministic nature of many static analyzers.

815	6   Conclusion
816	
817	In this study, we introduced the CASTLE benchmark, a curated collection of
818	250 compilable C micro-benchmarks covering 25 major CWEs. We proposed the
819	CASTLE Score to evaluate diverse vulnerability detection tools, including static
820	analyzers, formal verification methods, and large language models (LLMs). Our
821	work aimed to address the following research questions:
822	
823	 – RQ1: How do state-of-the-art static analysis tools, formal verification methods, and
824	   LLM-based approaches compare in effectively detecting vulnerabilities in C code?
825	   Answer: LLMs exhibit high effectiveness on compact code snippets, with GPT-
826	   o3-Mini scoring the highest (977 points) by identifying 126 out of 150 vulnerabili-
827	   ties. However, their performance declines on larger codebases, where false positives
828	   increase and hidden vulnerabilities often remain undetected. Static analyzers per-
829	   form moderately but produce numerous false positives, creating substantial manual
830	   triage overhead. Formal verification tools yield minimal false positives within their
831	   supported classes (e.g., memory safety) but cannot detect certain higher-level vul-
832	   nerabilities such as SQL injection, limiting their coverage.
833	 – RQ2: Are combinations of tools more effective than using a single tool?
834	   Answer: Tool combinations frequently outperform individual tools, particularly
835	   when they offset each other’s weaknesses. For instance, ESBMC (formal verifica-
836	   tion) combined with CodeQL achieved the highest two-tool CASTLE Score (814).
837	   Although overlapping detections can inflate false positives, well-chosen pairs lever-
838	   age complementary detection strategies, enhancing overall reliability.
839	 – RQ3: What metrics can reliably demonstrate these differences among various tools?
840	   Answer: As shown in Table 3, neither precision, accuracy, or recall could have pro-
841	   duced the same results and insights. The CASTLE Score integrates true positives,
842	   false positives, and CWE severity, providing a single, clear measure of tool perfor-
843	   mance. This setup enables transparent evaluation and straightforward comparisons
844	   across diverse methods, even for tool combinations.
845	
846	Implications and Future Work. Although micro-benchmarks efficiently re-
847	veal how tools behave on targeted vulnerabilities, they may not reflect the
848	full complexity of production-scale systems. Preliminary experiments show that
849	LLMs and formal verification tools both face significant scalability barriers when
850	analyzing large codebases. Ultimately, the insights gained through CASTLE un-
851	derscore the importance of selecting and combining tools to fit specific project
852	requirements rather than relying on any single method for comprehensive secu-
853	rity assurance.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] To introduce CASTLE (CWE Automated Security Testing and Low-Level Evaluation), a compilable, balanced, line-labelled C micro-benchmark, and use it to compare static analyzers, formal verification (FV) tools and LLMs for CWE detection, together with a new metric, the CASTLE Score (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: How do state-of-the-art static analysis tools, FV methods and LLM-based approaches compare in detecting C vulnerabilities? RQ2: Are combinations of tools more effective than a single tool? RQ3: What metrics can reliably show these differences? (p. 2).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus single-benchmark comparative evaluation of 25 tools/models (p. 6, p. 11).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 10 LLMs prompted via OpenAI-style APIs with one system prompt ("professional security analyst"), returning JSON with severity, line, CWE, message and line content; the prompt states "You get 5 points for each vulnerability you find, but get -1 for all false positives" (p. 8–9). [V] LLMs: GPT-o3-Mini, GPT-o1, DeepSeek R1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-Mini, Qwen 2.5 Coder Instruct 32B, Falcon 3 7B, Mistral Instruct 7B, Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B (Table 3, p. 11). No fine-tuning; zero-shot only.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Static analyzers with versions: CodeQL 2.20.1, GCC -fanalyzer 13.3.0, Snyk 1.1295.4, Semgrep Code 1.110.0, SonarQube 25.3.0, Coverity 2024.6.1, Cppcheck 2.13.0, Clang Analyzer 18.1.3, GitLab SAST 15.2.1, Splint 3.1.2, plus API-only Aikido, Jit, CodeThreat; FV tools ESBMC 7.8.1 and CBMC 5.95.1 (Table 3, p. 11). [V] ESBMC run with --overflow --no-unwinding-assertions --memory-leak-check --timeout 60 --multi-property (p. 12). [V] Tool combinations evaluated with a combination score (p. 10, p. 13). [I] No LLM + SAST/FV combination is evaluated (based on p. 11–13).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] 250 small C programs "crafted manually by cybersecurity experts"; each compiles (warnings allowed), single file, exactly one or zero vulnerabilities; vulnerable lines marked with `// {!LINE}` (p. 6–7).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 25 CWEs × 10 tests (6 vulnerable, 4 non-vulnerable) = 250 programs (150 vulnerable, 100 clean); 7–164 lines (mean 42, total 10,392); 1–8 functions; cyclomatic complexity 1–29 (mean 6.3); ~115,620 input tokens in total with the system prompt (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] CWEs chosen mostly from the MITRE Top-25 of 2023–2024; 7 of the 25 CWEs are not in the 2024 Top-25 (e.g., CWE-253, -327, -362, -401, -617, -628, -843) (Table 2, p. 7). [V] Iterative expert validation; ambiguous cases mapped to higher-level CWE (p. 6–7). Number and selection of experts: not reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] https://github.com/CASTLE-Benchmark (p. 1); wrappers public; intermediate vendor reports not shared (p. 9).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Free tools containerised in Docker with Python wrappers; closed-source tools (CodeThreat, Aikido) run via uploads to vendor dashboards/APIs with manual consistency checks (p. 8). [V] API-only tools and LLMs evaluated in February 2025 (p. 11). [V] LLM metadata and side-channel information removed before analysis (p. 7). [V] LLMs also return the code line content so that small line-number offsets could be adjusted during evaluation (p. 8). LLM temperature/sampling and model snapshot versions: not reported. Cost and runtime: not reported (only total token count, p. 6).
- Code availability: [V] Wrappers in the main repository (p. 9).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] TP, TN, FP, FN, precision, recall, accuracy (Table 3, p. 11). [V] CASTLE Score: per vulnerable test, correct detection scores 5 + Top-25 rank bonus (max 5) minus 1 per extra finding; per clean test with no report, 2 points; otherwise −(number of findings); missing a vulnerability with no report scores 0 (p. 9–10). Tools reporting nothing score 200; theoretical maximum 1,250 (p. 12). [V] Combination score: union of findings, TPs/TNs counted once, FP penalties summed (p. 10).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported. [A] Repeated evaluations deviate by less than 3% (p. 14); number of repeats not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Static/FV tools (TP/TN/FP/FN, P/R/A, CASTLE): ESBMC 53/91/32/97, 62%/35%/53%, 661; CodeQL 45/79/49/112, 48%/29%/44%, 634; GCC Fanalyzer 41/76/93/109, 31%/27%/37%, 559; Snyk 26/82/42/124, 38%/17%/39%, 552; Semgrep Code 36/73/70/120, 34%/23%/36%, 541; CBMC 18/100/0/132, 100%/12%/47%, 536; SonarQube 43/68/135/107, 24%/29%/31%, 511; Aikido 481; Jit 478; Coverity 31/86/62/119, 33%/21%/39%, 425; Cppcheck 19/100/9/131, 68%/13%/46%, 406; Clang Analyzer 13/99/2/137, 87%/9%/45%, 381; GitLab SAST 36/67/240/120, 13%/23%/22%, 374; Splint −598 (1,027 FP); CodeThreat −692 (1,101 FP) (Table 3, p. 11).
2. [V] LLMs: GPT-o3-Mini 126/60/73/36, 63%/78%/63%, 977; GPT-o1 128/56/90/35, 59%/78%/60%, 962; DeepSeek R1 148/41/166/17, 47%/90%/51%, 956; GPT-4o 136/45/116/43, 54%/76%/53%, 954; GPT-4o-Mini 134/27/263/43, 34%/76%/34%, 761; Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B 114/31/224/49, 34%/70%/35%, 708; Falcon 3 7B 521; Mistral 7B 446; Gemma 2 9B 436; Llama 3.1 8B 83/22/337/80, 20%/51%/20%, 417 (Table 3, p. 11).
3. [V] CodeQL is the best SAST tool, finding 29% (45/150) vs a 23% average among SAST tools; SonarQube also 29% but with 2.7× CodeQL's false positives (p. 12).
4. [A] Reasoning models (o1, o3-mini) produce fewer false positives than GPT-4o/4o-mini, which find more true positives (p. 14). [A] LLMs "rival—and often surpass" classical static analyzers on compact code (p. 14).
5. [V] Best two-tool combination ESBMC + CodeQL scores 814, +153 over ESBMC alone (661), i.e., +23% vs ESBMC and +28% vs CodeQL (p. 13). [A] Combinations help when tools have complementary CWE coverage; overlapping tools lose score through added FPs (p. 13).
6. [A] FV tools have very few FPs (CBMC 0) but cannot detect non-formal issues such as SQL injection, path traversal or hard-coded credentials (p. 12).
7. [A] Smaller models (<6B parameters) often failed to produce well-formed JSON; models often found the right vulnerability with an offset line number (p. 8).
8. [A] In a preliminary test on a 400+ line program built by merging clean tests, LLMs reported more false positives and most failed to find one hidden injected vulnerability (p. 14). No numbers given.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Micro-benchmark scope: single, isolated vulnerabilities; real software has cross-file flaws over many files (p. 14).
- [A] Lack of large code samples: LLM accuracy declines and false positives rise with code length; FV suffers state explosion; SAST scales better but has many FPs (p. 14).
- [A] Potential overfitting: fixed public tests could be targeted by vendors; dataset should be refreshed (p. 14).
- [A] LLM stochasticity, though repeated evaluations deviated less than 3% (p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Count inconsistencies in Table 3 (p. 11): there are 150 vulnerable programs, but TP + FN exceeds 150 for most LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o 136 + 43 = 179; DeepSeek R1 148 + 17 = 165) and for some tools (CodeQL 45 + 112 = 157, Semgrep 156, GitLab SAST 156, Jit 155). Recall therefore uses a denominator that is not the number of vulnerabilities (R1 recall 90% = 148/165, not 148/150), and accuracy is computed over finding counts rather than 250 programs. The counting rule for multiple findings per test is not explained. Exact recall/accuracy numbers should be quoted with this caveat.
- [I] The paper's own text is inconsistent on tool counts: "11 static code analyzers and 11 LLMs" (p. 3) vs 13 static + 2 FV + 10 LLMs (p. 1, p. 11).
- [I] Lenient LLM scoring: LLM line offsets were corrected using the returned line content (p. 8), a help not described for SAST tools; the prompt also mirrors the CASTLE scoring incentive (p. 9).
- [I] Synthetic, tiny, single-file programs (mean 42 lines) are ideal for LLM context windows and hard for tools tuned to real projects; the authors' own 400-line test suggests the ranking may flip on larger code (p. 14). This is the key external-validity caveat for RQ1.
- [I] The CASTLE Score is a new, author-defined weighting (bonus from Top-25 rank, 2 points per clean test, no penalty for silent misses) (p. 9–10). Its claim to be more reliable than precision/recall (p. 15) is not validated against any external criterion.
- [I] No per-CWE results table, so CWE-level strengths (RQ4) cannot be extracted beyond qualitative statements.
- [I] No LLM + static/FV hybrid is tested, though combination scoring would allow it.
- [I] LLM versions, temperature and costs not reported; closed models may change over time.
- [I] Funding partly from ZEISS Digital Innovation (p. 15); no conflict evident, noted for completeness. Several authors are ESBMC contributors/bug reporters (p. 12), and ESBMC ranks best among non-LLM tools.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Author-built tests and author-defined metric; line-offset correction for LLMs only; possible bias toward ESBMC-friendly memory-safety CWEs. Newly written tests reduce pre-training contamination, but tests are now public (p. 1).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] C only; single-file micro-programs; 25 CWEs with 10 tests each; no real-world code.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] CASTLE Score weights are arbitrary; TP/FN accounting inconsistent with the 150-vulnerability ground truth.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] 6 vulnerable tests per CWE; differences of a few TPs between tools are within noise; no CIs; LLM run-to-run variance only summarised (<3%).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Dataset and wrappers public with tool versions (p. 1, p. 9, p. 11); LLM settings and API-tool versions missing.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: refresh the dataset or use dynamic test generation to prevent overfitting (p. 14); study scalability to large codebases for LLMs and FV (p. 15); select and combine tools to fit project needs (p. 15); LLMs as real-time guidance in code-completion frameworks (p. 1).
- Suggested by us [I]: extend CASTLE to multi-file and larger programs with the same line-level labels; test LLM + FV/SAST hybrids with the combination score; publish per-CWE results and fix TP/FN accounting.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: The broadest tool panel in our set (13 SAST incl. commercial Coverity, Snyk, SonarQube; 2 FV; 10 LLMs incl. reasoning models) on one controlled C benchmark with line-level ground truth. It supports "frontier LLMs beat SAST on small self-contained code", while its own preliminary large-file test and table inconsistencies limit how far this can be generalised. Useful for RQ2 as a contrast to real-world repo-level studies (e.g., zhou2024comparison).

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Top LLMs outscore all static and FV tools on CASTLE: GPT-o3-Mini 977, GPT-o1 962, DeepSeek R1 956, GPT-4o 954 vs ESBMC 661, CodeQL 634 | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | LLM precision/recall: GPT-o3-Mini 63%/78%, GPT-4o 54%/76%, DeepSeek R1 47%/90%; small open models 20–28% precision | 11 | V | weak |
| RQ1 | SAST recall is low: CodeQL 29% (45/150), SAST average 23%; high-precision tools have very low recall (Clang 87%/9%, CBMC 100%/12%) | 11–12 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Some SAST tools are unusable from noise: Splint 1,027 FP and CodeThreat 1,101 FP, giving negative CASTLE scores | 11, 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Benchmark is 250 hand-written single-file C programs (mean 42 lines), balanced 150/100, line-labelled; differs strongly from real-world repo-level setups | 6 | V | strong |
| RQ2 | Table 3 TP+FN exceeds the 150 vulnerable programs for most LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o 179), so reported recall/accuracy use inconsistent denominators | 11 | I | moderate |
| RQ3 | Combining ESBMC and CodeQL raises the CASTLE score to 814 (+23% vs ESBMC); overlapping tools lose score through extra FPs; no LLM+tool hybrid tested | 10, 13 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Reasoning LLMs (o1, o3-mini) produce fewer FPs than GPT-4o/4o-mini | 11, 14 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | FV tools miss non-formal CWEs (SQL injection, path traversal, hard-coded credentials) but have near-zero FPs; no per-CWE numbers reported | 12 | A | weak |
| RQ4 | LLM accuracy declines and FPs rise on a 400+ line merged program; most LLMs missed a single hidden vulnerability | 14 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | Open problems: LLM scalability to large codebases, line-level localisation, JSON reliability of small models, benchmark overfitting | 8, 14 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "LLMs perform exceptionally well in the CASTLE dataset when identifying vulnerabilities in small code snippets. However, their accuracy declines, and hallucinations increase as the code size grows." (p. 1)

> "The best-performing SAST tool is CodeQL, which found 29% of the weaknesses in the code (45/150)" (p. 12)

> "most LLMs failed to detect it reliably, suggesting that these models' effectiveness may taper off with increasing code length." (p. 14)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1–18). Figures 1–3 are images; Fig. 2 combination labels are garbled in text extraction, so only the ESBMC + CodeQL combination (stated in text) is reported; other combination scores (697–758) are not attributed.
- Source version: arXiv v2 (2503.09433, 31 Mar 2025). Published version: book chapter in Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 2025 (DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-98208-8_15, from metadata; venue_kind "book", i.e., proceedings chapter). Metadata has no abstract; numbers could differ from the published chapter.
- Uncertainties: how multiple findings per test are counted in TP/FN (section 9); the exact LLM model snapshots; whether the published version corrected Table 3.

## zhou2024comparison · ready · full-text (arXiv v1, preprint, not peer-reviewed)
**Summary:** Compares 15 free SAST tools with 12 open LLMs of 8B parameters or less (fine-tuned, LoRA, zero-shot, CoT, few-shot) on whole repositories in Java, C and Python (270 CVEs). It reports no precision or F1, only detection ratios and the share of functions flagged. SAST detects up to 44.4% of CVEs while flagging 0.2–5.2% of functions; LLMs detect up to 100% but flag 3.5–77.4% of functions.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: best SAST is 37.5% (Horusec, Java), 44.4% (CodeQL, C), 30.0% (DevSkim, Python); many tools detect 0%. (p. 6–7, V, weak)
- RQ1: LLMs reach 90–100% detection but flag 3.5–77.4% of functions. (p. 6–7, V, weak)
- RQ1: LoRA fine-tuning beats prompting: Java 73.4% detection with 19.4% flagged. (p. 7, V, weak)
- RQ1: GPT-3.5 detects only 3.7–23.2%. (p. 10, V, weak)
- RQ2: vulnerable functions are 0.008–0.18% of all functions; flagged-function share is used as a stand-in for the false-positive rate. (p. 3, 5, V, moderate)
- RQ2: test sets are about 8–10 CVEs per language. (p. 6, I, weak)
- RQ3: running all SAST tools together raises detection by 25–100% relative to the best single tool. (p. 8, V, weak)
- RQ3: voting across LLMs cuts the flagged share by 40.9–74.6%. (p. 9, V, weak)
- RQ3: no SAST+LLM hybrid is tested. (I, moderate)
- RQ4: CWE-119 and CWE-476 are detected best; CWE-835 and CWE-89 are missed by both families. (p. 8, V, weak)
- RQ4: combined LLMs work best for Java, combined SAST for C and Python. (p. 9, A)
- RQ5: authors recommend filtering, repository context and repo-level evaluation. (p. 10, A)

**Problems found:**
- Table 3 contradicts the text and figures. It shows Horusec at 7.5 (text 37.5), CodeQL C at 4.4/3.3 (text 44.4/33.3) and DevSkim at 0.0/0.0 (text 30/20). I checked the rendered PDF and the cells are truncated there too.
- The abstract and conclusion say that ensembling SAST tools with LLMs reduces the drawbacks of both, but no such ensemble was run.
- Test sets are tiny, inferred from detection ratios that move in 12.5, 11.1 and 10-point steps.
- The split is random by CVE with no grouping by project, so the same project can appear in training and test.
- The "ESEC/FSE'23" page header is a template artefact, not a sign of publication.

## gnieciak2025large · ready · full-text (arXiv v1; published in IEEE Access 2025)
**Summary:** Compares SonarQube, CodeQL and Snyk Code (default settings) with zero-shot GPT-4.1, Mistral Large and DeepSeek V3 on 10 small C# projects with 63 vulnerabilities. Mean F1 is 0.797/0.753/0.750 for the LLMs vs 0.260/0.386/0.546 for the SAST tools; LLMs always give the wrong line or column and invent "outdated dependency" findings.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: mean F1 as above. (p. 10, V, weak)
- RQ1: mean recall is 0.78–0.88 for LLMs vs 0.19–0.52 for SAST; mean precision is 0.72–0.78 vs 0.57–0.69. (p. 10, V, weak)
- RQ1: pooling the raw counts (my arithmetic) gives SAST precision 0.81–0.87 vs LLM 0.74–0.79, and Snyk F1 about 0.70. (p. 8, I, weak)
- RQ2: LLMs get credit for findings at the wrong location; each tool ran once; projects were written by the authors. (p. 5–6, 8, V, moderate)
- RQ3: runtime per project is about 186–213 s for CodeQL, 14–29 s for Snyk and 3.5–67 s for the LLMs. (p. 9, V, weak)
- RQ3: authors recommend LLMs for early triage and SAST for audits, but test no hybrid. (A)
- RQ4: covers only C# SQLi, XSS, secrets, command injection, weak crypto and outdated dependencies, with no per-category results. (V, weak)
- RQ5: open problems are localisation and hallucinated findings. (p. 11–12, A)

**Problems found:**
- The abstract calls the projects "real-world", but the methods say they were "prepared" with "a random number of vulnerabilities" and are 3–5k characters each, which points to seeded test code.
- LLMs are credited for findings at the wrong line or column; SAST tools get no such allowance.
- When a tool reports nothing on a project, its precision is set to 0 and still averaged in, which drags SAST precision down.
- Pooled counts change the false-positive picture: GPT-4.1 has the most false positives (19), not DeepSeek. Snyk's share of false reports (15/57) is about the same as the LLMs'.
- The abstract mentions developer effort and a thematic analysis; neither is reported.
- Temperature, model versions and run cost are not reported. The paper refers to itself as "this thesis".

## khare2025understanding · ready · full-text (arXiv v3; published at ICST 2025)
**Summary:** Tests 16 LLMs with 3 prompts on 5,000 balanced single-function samples (OWASP, Juliet Java and C/C++, CVEFixes Java and C/C++; 25 CWEs). Compares them with CodeQL on the synthetic sets only, and with DeepDFA and LineVul on CVEFixes C/C++. The best LLM averages 62.8% accuracy; CodeQL beats the best LLM on accuracy on all synthetic sets, while LLMs win on specific CWEs.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: best LLM averages 62.8% accuracy; real-world accuracy is 10.5% lower than synthetic. (p. 5, V, moderate)
- RQ1: CodeQL vs best LLM, accuracy/F1: OWASP 0.63/0.72 vs 0.60/0.65; Juliet Java 0.94/0.94 vs 0.76/0.79; Juliet C/C++ 0.72/0.61 vs 0.65/0.72. (p. 9, V, moderate)
- RQ1: on CVEFixes C/C++, Qwen-2.5-32B has F1 0.65 vs DeepDFA 0.23 and LineVul 0.61 (both trained on the same dataset); LineVul trained on BigVul drops to F1 0.02. (p. 10, V, moderate)
- RQ1: larger models are not reliably better. (p. 5, A)
- RQ2: many configurations answer "vulnerable" every time (precision 0.50, recall 1.00, F1 0.67), which is the trivial result on a 50/50 set. (p. 16, I, moderate)
- RQ2: CodeQL is run on synthetic data only, and the best LLM is picked after seeing results from 48 configurations. (V, moderate)
- RQ3: a dataflow-style prompt raises real-world F1 by up to 0.18; sources and sinks are correct in 16–18 of 20 checked samples. (p. 5–6, V, weak)
- RQ3: authors propose LLMs finding sources/sinks for a static analyser to reason over. (A)
- RQ4: LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-22, 78, 476 and 416 (up to +24%); CodeQL is better on CWE-190 (+11–21%). (p. 8, V, moderate)
- RQ4: LLMs do well on self-contained CWEs and poorly on context-dependent ones (CWE-862, C/C++ out-of-bounds). (p. 7, V, moderate)
- RQ5: missing global context is the main failure cause. (p. 7, A)

**Problems found:**
- The headline F1 of 0.71 is barely above the always-"vulnerable" result of 0.67.
- The abstract says LLMs beat CodeQL; that holds only for certain CWEs, not overall.
- Table V lists DSCoder-15B with a size of "33B".
- The appendix wording on CVEFixes labels reads as reversed.
- No cost data, and no code or data link in this version.

## dubniczky2025castle · ready · full-text (arXiv v2; published as an LNCS chapter, venue_kind "book"; metadata has no abstract)
**Summary:** Introduces CASTLE, 250 hand-written single-file C programs (mean 42 lines, 25 CWEs, 150 vulnerable and 100 clean). Evaluates 13 static analysers, 2 formal verification tools and 10 LLMs using a new author-defined CASTLE Score. GPT-o3-mini scores 977, o1 962, R1 956 and GPT-4o 954, vs ESBMC 661 and CodeQL 634; the authors warn that LLM results drop on larger code.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: the CASTLE scores above. (p. 11, V, moderate)
- RQ1: LLM precision/recall: o3-mini 63%/78%, GPT-4o 54%/76%, R1 47%/90%; small open models have 20–28% precision. (V, weak)
- RQ1: CodeQL finds 29% (45/150) vs a 23% SAST average; Clang 87%/9% and CBMC 100%/12% precision/recall. (p. 11–12, V, moderate)
- RQ1: Splint and CodeThreat report more than 1,000 false positives each. (V, moderate)
- RQ2: benchmark design (single-file, balanced, line-labelled). (p. 6, V, strong)
- RQ2: TP+FN exceeds the 150 vulnerable programs for most LLMs. (p. 11, I, moderate)
- RQ3: ESBMC + CodeQL scores 814 (+23%); no LLM+tool hybrid is tested. (p. 13, V, weak)
- RQ3: reasoning models produce fewer false positives. (V, weak)
- RQ4: formal verification misses SQLi, path traversal and credentials; no per-CWE numbers are given. (p. 12, A)
- RQ4: on a 400+ line file, LLM false positives rise and most models miss the hidden bug. (p. 14, A, no numbers)
- RQ5: scalability, localisation and benchmark overfitting. (A)

**Problems found:**
- Table 3 counts don't add up: GPT-4o has 136 TP + 43 FN = 179 and R1 has 165 against 150 vulnerable programs. CodeQL (157), Semgrep, GitLab and Jit also exceed 150. Recall and accuracy therefore use inconsistent denominators.
- The text gives conflicting tool counts: "11 static and 11 LLMs" on p. 3 vs 13+2+10.
- LLM line-number offsets were corrected using the code line they returned; SAST tools got no such help. The prompt also tells models how they will be scored.
- The CASTLE Score's weights are the authors' own and are not checked against anything external.
- The authors filed ESBMC bug reports and earlier work by co-authors used ESBMC; ESBMC tops the non-LLM tools.

## Across the four papers
- None of them actually tests an LLM+SAST hybrid, though all recommend one, so the RQ3 evidence is opinion only.
- The direction of the result depends on code size and setup:
  - Small or synthetic snippets favour LLMs (gnieciak2025large, dubniczky2025castle).
  - Whole real repositories give LLMs high detection but very noisy output (zhou2024comparison).
  - CodeQL still wins on Juliet and OWASP (khare2025understanding).

  This is a candidate entry for the RQ2 contradiction section.

## zhou2024comparison · ready · full-text (arXiv v1, preprint, not peer-reviewed)
**Summary:** Compares 15 free SAST tools with 12 open LLMs of 8B parameters or less (fine-tuned, LoRA, zero-shot, CoT, few-shot) on whole repositories in Java, C and Python (270 CVEs). It reports no precision or F1, only detection ratios and the share of functions flagged. SAST detects up to 44.4% of CVEs while flagging 0.2–5.2% of functions; LLMs detect up to 100% but flag 3.5–77.4% of functions.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: best SAST is 37.5% (Horusec, Java), 44.4% (CodeQL, C), 30.0% (DevSkim, Python); many tools detect 0%. (p. 6–7, V, weak)
- RQ1: LLMs reach 90–100% detection but flag 3.5–77.4% of functions. (p. 6–7, V, weak)
- RQ1: LoRA fine-tuning beats prompting: Java 73.4% detection with 19.4% flagged. (p. 7, V, weak)
- RQ1: GPT-3.5 detects only 3.7–23.2%. (p. 10, V, weak)
- RQ2: vulnerable functions are 0.008–0.18% of all functions; flagged-function share is used as a stand-in for the false-positive rate. (p. 3, 5, V, moderate)
- RQ2: test sets are about 8–10 CVEs per language. (p. 6, I, weak)
- RQ3: running all SAST tools together raises detection by 25–100% relative to the best single tool. (p. 8, V, weak)
- RQ3: voting across LLMs cuts the flagged share by 40.9–74.6%. (p. 9, V, weak)
- RQ3: no SAST+LLM hybrid is tested. (I, moderate)
- RQ4: CWE-119 and CWE-476 are detected best; CWE-835 and CWE-89 are missed by both families. (p. 8, V, weak)
- RQ4: combined LLMs work best for Java, combined SAST for C and Python. (p. 9, A)
- RQ5: authors recommend filtering, repository context and repo-level evaluation. (p. 10, A)

**Problems found:**
- Table 3 contradicts the text and figures. It shows Horusec at 7.5 (text 37.5), CodeQL C at 4.4/3.3 (text 44.4/33.3) and DevSkim at 0.0/0.0 (text 30/20). I checked the rendered PDF and the cells are truncated there too.
- The abstract and conclusion say that ensembling SAST tools with LLMs reduces the drawbacks of both, but no such ensemble was run.
- Test sets are tiny, inferred from detection ratios that move in 12.5, 11.1 and 10-point steps.
- The split is random by CVE with no grouping by project, so the same project can appear in training and test.
- The "ESEC/FSE'23" page header is a template artefact, not a sign of publication.

## gnieciak2025large · ready · full-text (arXiv v1; published in IEEE Access 2025)
**Summary:** Compares SonarQube, CodeQL and Snyk Code (default settings) with zero-shot GPT-4.1, Mistral Large and DeepSeek V3 on 10 small C# projects with 63 vulnerabilities. Mean F1 is 0.797/0.753/0.750 for the LLMs vs 0.260/0.386/0.546 for the SAST tools; LLMs always give the wrong line or column and invent "outdated dependency" findings.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: mean F1 as above. (p. 10, V, weak)
- RQ1: mean recall is 0.78–0.88 for LLMs vs 0.19–0.52 for SAST; mean precision is 0.72–0.78 vs 0.57–0.69. (p. 10, V, weak)
- RQ1: pooling the raw counts (my arithmetic) gives SAST precision 0.81–0.87 vs LLM 0.74–0.79, and Snyk F1 about 0.70. (p. 8, I, weak)
- RQ2: LLMs get credit for findings at the wrong location; each tool ran once; projects were written by the authors. (p. 5–6, 8, V, moderate)
- RQ3: runtime per project is about 186–213 s for CodeQL, 14–29 s for Snyk and 3.5–67 s for the LLMs. (p. 9, V, weak)
- RQ3: authors recommend LLMs for early triage and SAST for audits, but test no hybrid. (A)
- RQ4: covers only C# SQLi, XSS, secrets, command injection, weak crypto and outdated dependencies, with no per-category results. (V, weak)
- RQ5: open problems are localisation and hallucinated findings. (p. 11–12, A)

**Problems found:**
- The abstract calls the projects "real-world", but the methods say they were "prepared" with "a random number of vulnerabilities" and are 3–5k characters each, which points to seeded test code.
- LLMs are credited for findings at the wrong line or column; SAST tools get no such allowance.
- When a tool reports nothing on a project, its precision is set to 0 and still averaged in, which drags SAST precision down.
- Pooled counts change the false-positive picture: GPT-4.1 has the most false positives (19), not DeepSeek. Snyk's share of false reports (15/57) is about the same as the LLMs'.
- The abstract mentions developer effort and a thematic analysis; neither is reported.
- Temperature, model versions and run cost are not reported. The paper refers to itself as "this thesis".

## khare2025understanding · ready · full-text (arXiv v3; published at ICST 2025)
**Summary:** Tests 16 LLMs with 3 prompts on 5,000 balanced single-function samples (OWASP, Juliet Java and C/C++, CVEFixes Java and C/C++; 25 CWEs). Compares them with CodeQL on the synthetic sets only, and with DeepDFA and LineVul on CVEFixes C/C++. The best LLM averages 62.8% accuracy; CodeQL beats the best LLM on accuracy on all synthetic sets, while LLMs win on specific CWEs.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: best LLM averages 62.8% accuracy; real-world accuracy is 10.5% lower than synthetic. (p. 5, V, moderate)
- RQ1: CodeQL vs best LLM, accuracy/F1: OWASP 0.63/0.72 vs 0.60/0.65; Juliet Java 0.94/0.94 vs 0.76/0.79; Juliet C/C++ 0.72/0.61 vs 0.65/0.72. (p. 9, V, moderate)
- RQ1: on CVEFixes C/C++, Qwen-2.5-32B has F1 0.65 vs DeepDFA 0.23 and LineVul 0.61 (both trained on the same dataset); LineVul trained on BigVul drops to F1 0.02. (p. 10, V, moderate)
- RQ1: larger models are not reliably better. (p. 5, A)
- RQ2: many configurations answer "vulnerable" every time (precision 0.50, recall 1.00, F1 0.67), which is the trivial result on a 50/50 set. (p. 16, I, moderate)
- RQ2: CodeQL is run on synthetic data only, and the best LLM is picked after seeing results from 48 configurations. (V, moderate)
- RQ3: a dataflow-style prompt raises real-world F1 by up to 0.18; sources and sinks are correct in 16–18 of 20 checked samples. (p. 5–6, V, weak)
- RQ3: authors propose LLMs finding sources/sinks for a static analyser to reason over. (A)
- RQ4: LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-22, 78, 476 and 416 (up to +24%); CodeQL is better on CWE-190 (+11–21%). (p. 8, V, moderate)
- RQ4: LLMs do well on self-contained CWEs and poorly on context-dependent ones (CWE-862, C/C++ out-of-bounds). (p. 7, V, moderate)
- RQ5: missing global context is the main failure cause. (p. 7, A)

**Problems found:**
- The headline F1 of 0.71 is barely above the always-"vulnerable" result of 0.67.
- The abstract says LLMs beat CodeQL; that holds only for certain CWEs, not overall.
- Table V lists DSCoder-15B with a size of "33B".
- The appendix wording on CVEFixes labels reads as reversed.
- No cost data, and no code or data link in this version.

## dubniczky2025castle · ready · full-text (arXiv v2; published as an LNCS chapter, venue_kind "book"; metadata has no abstract)
**Summary:** Introduces CASTLE, 250 hand-written single-file C programs (mean 42 lines, 25 CWEs, 150 vulnerable and 100 clean). Evaluates 13 static analysers, 2 formal verification tools and 10 LLMs using a new author-defined CASTLE Score. GPT-o3-mini scores 977, o1 962, R1 956 and GPT-4o 954, vs ESBMC 661 and CodeQL 634; the authors warn that LLM results drop on larger code.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: the CASTLE scores above. (p. 11, V, moderate)
- RQ1: LLM precision/recall: o3-mini 63%/78%, GPT-4o 54%/76%, R1 47%/90%; small open models have 20–28% precision. (V, weak)
- RQ1: CodeQL finds 29% (45/150) vs a 23% SAST average; Clang 87%/9% and CBMC 100%/12% precision/recall. (p. 11–12, V, moderate)
- RQ1: Splint and CodeThreat report more than 1,000 false positives each. (V, moderate)
- RQ2: benchmark design (single-file, balanced, line-labelled). (p. 6, V, strong)
- RQ2: TP+FN exceeds the 150 vulnerable programs for most LLMs. (p. 11, I, moderate)
- RQ3: ESBMC + CodeQL scores 814 (+23%); no LLM+tool hybrid is tested. (p. 13, V, weak)
- RQ3: reasoning models produce fewer false positives. (V, weak)
- RQ4: formal verification misses SQLi, path traversal and credentials; no per-CWE numbers are given. (p. 12, A)
- RQ4: on a 400+ line file, LLM false positives rise and most models miss the hidden bug. (p. 14, A, no numbers)
- RQ5: scalability, localisation and benchmark overfitting. (A)

**Problems found:**
- Table 3 counts don't add up: GPT-4o has 136 TP + 43 FN = 179 and R1 has 165 against 150 vulnerable programs. CodeQL (157), Semgrep, GitLab and Jit also exceed 150. Recall and accuracy therefore use inconsistent denominators.
- The text gives conflicting tool counts: "11 static and 11 LLMs" on p. 3 vs 13+2+10.
- LLM line-number offsets were corrected using the code line they returned; SAST tools got no such help. The prompt also tells models how they will be scored.
- The CASTLE Score's weights are the authors' own and are not checked against anything external.
- The authors filed ESBMC bug reports and earlier work by co-authors used ESBMC; ESBMC tops the non-LLM tools.

## Across the four papers
- None of them actually tests an LLM+SAST hybrid, though all recommend one, so the RQ3 evidence is opinion only.
- The direction of the result depends on code size and setup:
  - Small or synthetic snippets favour LLMs (gnieciak2025large, dubniczky2025castle).
  - Whole real repositories give LLMs high detection but very noisy output (zhou2024comparison).
  - CodeQL still wins on Juliet and OWASP (khare2025understanding).

  This is a candidate entry for the RQ2 contradiction section.
